case_name: Service Employees International Union, Local 333 v. North Central Health District Board
text:
S.E.I.U., Local 333 v. North Central Health Dist. Board

1997-01-14

Saskatchewan Queen's Bench

CHRR Doc. 97-047

Service Employees International Union, Local 333

Applicant (Interested Party)

v.

North Central Health District Board

Respondent (Applicant)

and

Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

Respondent

Date of Decision:

January 14, 1997

Before:

Saskatchewan Queen's Bench, Barclay J.

Court File No.:

Q.B. No. 809 (Saskatoon)

Appeal from:

(sub nom. North Central Health Dist. Board (Re))

(1995),
1995 CanLII 10833 (SK HRT)
,
28 C.H.R.R. D/61 (Sask. H.R.Comm.)

Appearances by:

Lorraine L. St. Cyr, Counsel for the Applicant

Melissa Brunsdon, Counsel for the Respondent North Central Health Dist. Board

EXEMPTIONS — gender — BONA FIDE OCCUPATIONAL QUALIFICATION — gender for healthcare worker

PUBLIC DECENCY — gender preference for healthcare worker — SEX DISCRIMINATION — employment terminated for gender — healthcare worker position denied

ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNALS — standard of review of court over administrative tribunal — APPEALS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW — reasons for decision under review are patently unreasonable

Summary:
This is an appeal by the Service Employees International Union ("SEIU") from the decision of the Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission to extend an exemption originally granted in 1989 to two special care homes in Melfort, Saskatchewan. The exemption permits the Nirvana Pioneer Villa, which is the only one of the homes that continues to operate, to designate 3.5 attendant care positions for men only.

The North Central Health District Board argues that this exemption is necessary to allow the Villa to offer residents some choice regarding the gender of the attendants who provide intimate personal care. The SEIU submits, however, that the exemption permits unlawful discrimination against female employees and prospective female employees of the Villa.

At the outset, the Court finds that, following the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15, the standard of review for decisions made by human rights tribunals is whether the decision was patently unreasonable.

The Court confirms the reasoning of the Commission, finding that it has appropriately balanced the right of employees to be free from discrimination against the right of residents to be free from the application of the
Code
in their personal lives, in particular where attendant care involves intimate physical touching and assistance with bathing and toiletting.

The application is dismissed with costs.

[
1
]    This is an application by the Service Employees International Union, Local 333 ("SEIU"), for judicial review of a decision of the Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission (the "Commission").

[
2
]    The Commission had granted an exemption under
s. 16(1)
of
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code,
S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, as amended (the "
Code
") [reported
1995 CanLII 10833 (SK HRT)
,
28 C.H.R.R. D/61
]. to the North Central District Health Board (the "Board"), who were operating Nirvana Pioneer Villa ("Nirvana"), a nursing home in Melfort, Saskatchewan, to permit it to advertise and hire men in 3.5 attendant positions in order to give male residents a choice as to the gender of their personal care attendants.

FACTS

[
3
]    Nirvana is a level III and IV special care home in Melfort.

[
4
]    The Melfort and District Pioneer Lodge (the "Lodge") was a Level II special care home in Melfort. The Lodge was operating in 1988 but was subsequently closed in October 1994.

[
5
]    In 1988, the Melfort and District Pioneer Home was the employer at both Nirvana and the Lodge (collectively referred to as the "Homes"). It was controlled by an autonomous governing board of directors.

[
6
]    The Board succeeded the Melfort and District Pioneer Home in 1991. Since that time the Board has managed health facilities in Melfort. The Board was responsible for the closure of the Lodge in October 1994, but continues to operate Nirvana.

[
7
]    SEIU represented the employees at both Nirvana and the Lodge in 1988 and continues to represent employees at Nirvana.

[
8
]    In 1988, the Homes asked the Commission for an exemption from
s. 16(1)
of the
Code
in order to fill a vacant resident attendant position with a man. The Homes sought this exemption in order to provide residents with more choice about the gender of the attendants providing their personal care.

[
9
]    On January 10, 1989, the Commission granted the exemption requested and permitted the Homes to designate one resident attendant position as male-only in order to fill the vacancy. This allowed the Homes to increase the total number of positions held by male attendants to 2.5.

[
10
]    In 1991, the Homes sought to expand the number of male resident attendants, by filling vacant positions with men until they reached their goal of 4.5 full-time male resident attendants. The Homes applied to the Commission to increase the exemption to 4.5. The purpose of this application was to accommodate requests by family members and residents that the residents have a choice regarding the gender of their caregiver and to provide this choice on a long-term basis.

[
11
]    On November 13, 1991, after an oral hearing, the Commission granted the exemption pursuant to s. 48 of the
Code
and allowed the Homes to advertise and to hire male resident attendants, as positions became vacant, until there were 4.5 male full-time equivalent resident attendants. SEIU opposed the application at the oral hearing. The exemption order was to continue in effect until November 30, 1995.

[
12
]    In October 1994, following the closure of the Lodge, the Board voluntarily reduced the exemption to 3.5 by eliminating one male-only resident position.

[
13
]    On November 25, 1994, SEIU requested a reconsideration of the exemption, pursuant to
s. 47(2)
of the
Code
in a letter to the Director of the Commission. It is unclear whether the SEIU intended the request to be made under s. 48(2) rather than
s. 47(2)
.

[
14
]    The Director notified the Homes of the reconsideration request in a letter dated December 16, 1994. The Board was informed of the request on February 21, 1995. The Board responded on March 30, 1995, by indicating in a letter to the Commission that they believed the exemption order remained necessary to satisfy requests from family members and residents that they have a choice regarding the gender of the attendant providing personal care.

[
15
]    As the exemption order was to expire on November 30,1995, the Board and SEIU agreed with the Commission that the reconsideration request of SEIU should be treated as a request by the Board for an extension of the exemption. Neither the Board nor SEIU requested the Commission to hold an oral hearing.

[
16
]    The Commission considered the application for an extension of the order at its August 24, 1995, meeting. Both parties filed material supporting their position and were allowed to respond to the other side's submissions.

[
17
]    At the time of the meeting of the Commission, Nirvana accommodated twenty male residents and thirty-seven female residents. Nirvana had 21.05 attendant positions, 3.5 of which were designated as male attendant positions pursuant to the exemption order and as voluntarily reduced by the Board.

[
18
]    The decision and order of the Commission was issued on October 27, 1995. The Commission granted the Board's application for an extension of the exemption pursuant to s. 48 of the
Code
and ordered that it continue until October 27, 1997. The exemption, however, was formally reduced to permit the Board to advertise and hire men in 3.5 attendant positions at Nirvana, rather than 4.5 attendant positions. It is this decision and order which is the subject matter of this application.

THE SASKATCHEWAN HUMAN RIGHTS CODE

[
19
]    The relevant sections of the
Code
are:

16(1) No employer shall refuse to employ or continue to employ or otherwise discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to employment, or any term or condition of employment, because of his or their race, creed, religion, colour, sex, sexual orientation, family status, marital status, disability, age, nationality, ancestry, place of origin or receipt of public assistance.

(7) The provisions of this section relating to any discrimination, limitation, specification or preference for a position or employment based on sex, disability or age do not apply where sex, ability or age is a reasonable occupational qualification and requirement for the position or employment.

48(1) Where any person or class of persons is entitled to an exemption under any provision of this Act or any other Act administered by the commission or where the commission or the Director of Human Rights considers it necessary and advisable, the commission or the Director of Human Rights may, upon application from the person who is entitled to the exemption or who seeks the exemption, by order made in accordance with any terms, conditions or criteria prescribed in the regulations, exempt that person or class of persons from any or all of the provisions of this Act, other than Part I, or from any or all of the provisions of any other Act administered by the commission.

(2) Notwithstanding that an exemption order has been made under subsection (1), the commission may, on its own initiative or upon application from any person or class of persons, terminate the exemption order, but the person or class of persons in whose favour the exemption order was made shall receive thirty days' written notice that the exemption order may be terminated and shall be allowed to make representation to the commission.

(3) Notice under subsection (2) may be given personally, by registered mail addressed to the last known postal address of the persons in whose favour the exemption order was made, or by publishing that notice on three consecutive days in the daily newspaper published closest to the places of residence of those persons.

ISSUES

20 1.    What is the appropriate standard of judicial review?

2.    Did the Commission make a jurisdictional error, or in the alternative, arrive at a patently unreasonable interpretation, in failing to apply the reasonable occupational qualification provision found in
s. 16(7)
of the
Code
in determining that an exemption from
s. 16(1)
of the
Code
was warranted?

3.    Did the Commission commit an error of law apparent on the face of the record in determining that
s. 48
of the
Code
was applicable for adjudicating such an exemption request?

4.    Did the Commission make an error of law in determining that the Board discharged the burden of proof required to justify the exemption pursuant to
s. 48
of the
Code
?

5.    Did the Commission make an error of law in failing to determine that such exemption was "necessary and advisable" as required by the provisions of
s. 48
of the
Code
?

6.    Did the Commission make a jurisdictional error in determining that the provisions of the
Code
protect private rights and therefore ought to be extended to residents who live within institutions through recognition of their preferences?

1.    What is the appropriate standard of judicial review?

21    Although there was some confusion as to the appropriate standard of review for decisions of human rights commissions, and in particular the amount of deference that should be afforded by the courts to these tribunals, the matter has now been conclusively decided by the recent decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Ross
v.
New Brunswick School District No. 15
,

1996 CanLII 237 (SCC)
,
[1996] 1 S.C.R. 825
[25 C.H.R.R. D/175]. In this case a teacher publicly made racist and discriminatory comments against Jews during his off-duty time. His writings and statements communicated his anti-Semitic views including four books or pamphlets, letters to a local newspaper, and a local television interview. A complaint was filed with the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission. The Commission [
sic
] found that the teacher's off-duty comments denigrated the faith and belief of Jews and that the School Board which employed the teacher was guilty of discrimination by failing to meaningfully discipline him. The Commission [
sic
] directed the School Board to comply with the following: (a) place R. on a leave of absence without pay for a period of eighteen months; (b) appoint him to a non-teaching position, if one became available during that period; (c) terminate his employment at the end of that period if, in the interim, he had not been offered and accepted a non-teaching position; and (d) terminate his employment with the School Board immediately if he published or wrote anti-Semitic materials or sold his previous publications any time during the leave of absence period or at any time during his employment in a non-teaching position. The Court of Queen's Bench allowed the teacher's application for judicial review in part, ordering that clause 2(d) of the order be quashed on the ground that it was in excess of jurisdiction. The Court also concluded that para. 2 of the order violated
ss. 2(a)
and
2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
but that, with the exception of
clause 2(d)
, it could be saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the cross appeals with respect to clause 2(d), and allowed the teacher's appeal, holding that clauses 2(a), (b) and (c) of the order infringed R.'s freedom of expression and freedom of religion, and could not be justified under s. 1. The Supreme Court of Canada allowed the appeal and clauses 2(a), (b) and (c) of the order were restored.

[22]    The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada is of importance as it raises two general issues in relation to the standard of judicial review. The first relates to the standard of deference to be applied to the Commission's [
sic
] finding of discrimination and its remedial order. The second relates to the standard of constitutional review to be applied to the Board's order.

[23]    With respect to the administrative law issue, the superior expertise of a human rights tribunal is confined to fact finding and decision making in the context of human rights and therefore, reasonableness is the test for judicial review. However, if the issue is one of law, the standard of review is one of correctness.

[24]    In other words, the appropriate standard of review by a superior court of a factual determination is whether the decision is patently unreasonable. La Forest J.,
in
Ross
,
stated at p. 847 [D/185, para. 24]:

On the basis of this difference between human rights tribunals and labour tribunals, the Court confined the superior expertise of a human rights tribunal to fact-finding and adjudication in a human rights context. The standard of review on the basis of reasonableness is applicable to these matters ...

[25]    Where a human rights commission is required to interpret laws of general application, the correctness test applies. In the Supreme Court of Canada
decision in
Canada (Attorney General)
v.
Mossop

(1993),
1993 CanLII 164 (SCC)
,
13 Admin. L.R. (2d) 1
[17 C.H.R.R. D/349], which was
cited with approval in
Ross
,
La Forest J. stated at 28 [D/365, para. 43]:

... The superior expertise of a human rights tribunal relates to fact-finding and adjudication in a human rights context. It does not extend to general questions of law such as the one at issue in this case. These are ultimately matters within the province of the judiciary, and involve concepts of statutory interpretation and general legal reasoning which the courts must be supposed competent to perform. The courts cannot abdicate this duty to the tribunal. They must, therefore, review the tribunal's decisions on questions of this kind on the basis of correctness, not on a standard of reasonability.

[26]    The Supreme Court of Canada's
decision in
Ross
concerning "jurisdictional facts" has extended the deference provided to a human rights commission to include not only the "jurisdictional facts" upon which the legal question is decided, but also the legal question itself. This proposition was asserted by La Forest J., speaking for the unanimous full Court at p. 849 [D/187, paras. 28–29]:

... The expertise of the tribunals appointed under their aegis is limited to fact-finding and adjudication in human rights matters. In the process of performing its adjudicative function, a human rights tribunal will be called on to apply general legal reasoning and statutory interpretation, matters which are ultimately within the province of the judiciary.

That having been said, I do not think the fact-finding expertise of human rights tribunals should be restrictively interpreted, and it must be assessed against the backdrop of the particular decision the tribunal is called upon to make. Here, inquiry into the appropriate standard of review is largely governed by the fact that the administrative law issue raised calls upon this Court to consider whether the finding of discrimination by the Board of Inquiry was beyond its jurisdiction. A finding of discrimination is impregnated with facts, facts which the Board of Inquiry is in the best position to evaluate. The Board heard considerable evidence relating to the allegation of discrimination and was required to assess the credibility of the witnesses' evidence and draw inferences from the factual evidence presented to it in making a determination as to the existence of discrimination. Given the complexity of the evidentiary inferences made on the basis of the facts before the Board, it is appropriate to exercise a relative degree of deference to the finding of discrimination, in light of the Board's superior expertise in fact-finding, a conclusion supported by the existence of words importing a limited privative effect into the constituent legislation.

[27]    In this case, although the Board's application for an exemption pursuant to s. 48 involves a determination of a question of law, I agree with counsel for the Board that the standard of review is one of reasonableness since that question would be determined by the Commission's findings of fact.

[28]    Furthermore, where the legislation confers a discretion on an administrative tribunal such [as] a human rights commission, the standard of review is whether or not the decision is patently unreasonable.

2.    Did the Commission make a jurisdictional error, or in the alternative, arrive at a patently unreasonable interpretation, in failing to apply the reasonable occupational qualification provision found in
s. 16(7)
of the
Code
in determining that an exemption from
s. 16(1)
of the Code was warranted?

[29]    In this case the Commission stated as follows at p. 5 of its decision [D/62–D/63, para. 9]:

This exemption order falls into a category of exemptions relating to employment that protect the personal dignity and autonomy of individuals who live in institutions. The category involves a balancing of two fundamental
Code
objectives. On the one hand, the
Code
aims to promote equality of individuals by prohibiting discrimination in many aspects of community life, including employment, and permitting measures to overcome inequalities. This fundamental objective underlies the entire
Code.
At the same time, it aims to protect the dignity and autonomy of individuals. This objective also underlies the
Code.
In a recent decision,
Regina Pioneer Village and Zapototsky
(1994), 94 C.L.L.C. para. 17,039, the Commission commented on the relationship between these two basic principles in the context of personal care:

On the basis of this principle, the Commission has granted a number of exemptions involving the personal care of individuals confined to institutions. For instance, several nursing homes have exemptions that permit them to hire a man or a woman (as required by circumstances) in order to offer residents a choice about the sex of employees providing personal care. Personal care involves bodily functions of an intimate nature, such as toiletry, bathing, and for non-elderly female residents, assistance with sanitary products during menstruation. Residents in facilities have already lost a great deal of autonomy in their personal lives. Respect for their inherent dignity compels offering them a choice, if possible, about the sex of their personal caregiver. Offering residents a choice may interfere with the right of employees to be treated equally regardless of sex, since one sex will be preferred for a limited number of positions. But the interference is justified by the importance of respecting the dignity and autonomy, in a most intimate area of daily life, of individuals with very little power and few other choices.

Other facilities with similar exemptions are correctional centres (to permit same-sex employees to conduct strip searches and searches of bodily cavities) and group homes.

[30]    Section 16(1) prevents an employer from engaging in discriminatory practices with respect to employment. Under s. 48(1), the Commission may grant an exemption from s. 16(1) where the Commission considers it "necessary and advisable". In
Regina Pioneer Village
[(1994), 94 C.L.L.C. para. 17,039,
1994 CanLII 10754 (SK HRT)
,
23 C.H.R.R. D/25
], the Commission referred to "two broad types of justifications" where an exemption will be considered by the Commission to be "necessary and advisable" (at pp. 16,443 and 16,444 [D/27, paras. 9 and 12]).

1.    Where the exemption would advance the objects of the
Code
,
as set out in
s. 3
, namely:

(a)   the promotion of equality; or

(b)   the promotion of the inherent dignity and autonomy of the individual.

2.    Where the exemption advances another meritorious or compelling social policy not found in the
Code
or attainable by any other methods with less discriminatory impact.

[31]    With respect to the first justification, the two objects of the
Code
may, in some instances, conflict, and therefore it is necessary for the Commission to balance the competing interests protected by these objects when considering whether an exemption to s. 16(1) should be granted. As neither object is determinative of whether an exemption should be granted, the party seeking the exemption must establish that on balance the objects favour the granting of the exemption.

[32]    The second justification is much narrower than the first since the "compelling social policy" sought to be advanced by the exemption lies outside of the
Code
.

[33]    The Commission granted an exemption on the basis of a "compelling social policy"
in
Saskatchewan (Agriculture and Food) (Re)

(1994),
1994 CanLII 10760 (SK HRT)
,
23 C.H.R.R. D/19
. In this decision Saskatchewan Agriculture and Food sought the exemption from
s. 10(1)
of the
Code
in order to pursue a policy of giving younger farmers some preference when allocating leases of Crown land to farmers. The two reasons accepted by the Commission in granting the exemption were firstly, as younger farmers are economically disadvantaged compared to older farmers and account for only a small portion of the total farmers in Saskatchewan, the exemption would be consistent with the goal of promoting equality. Secondly, encouraging younger farmers helps the future of agriculture in Saskatchewan by sustaining the number of family farms and by maintaining a diverse rural population that contributes to a more vibrant rural life and agricultural economy.

[34]    With respect to the second reason, the Commission commented in
Regina Pioneer Village,
at p. 16,444 [D/27, para. 13]:

This reason falls into the second category of justification. While a vibrant farm economy may not be directly connected to the principles of equality and autonomy underlying the
Code
,
it is a compelling objective in a province dependent on agriculture for its citizens' quality of life

[35]    In the
Regina Pioneer Village
decision at p. 16,444 [D/28], the Commission referred to two types of justifications that an employer could bring forward to establish that a person's gender was a "reasonable occupational qualification" for a job. These two justifications were said to exist when (1) the preference for one sex is required by the essential functions of the job; or (2) restricting a position to one gender is required by an overriding objective of the
Code
.
With respect to this second justification, the Commission stated at p. 16,444 [D/28, para. 16]: "The exemption decisions about personal care of residents fall into this category ..."

[36]    When determining whether an exemption should be granted under s. 48, the Commission may take into consideration all of the exceptions and defences permitted by the
Code
as a whole. However, where an applicant for an exemption relies on an overriding object of the
Code
to justify the exemption, it is not necessary for the Commission to apply these exceptions and defences. Rather the Commission may simply engage in a balancing of the two objects of the
Code.

[37]    If it is SEIU's position that
s. 16(7)
must be satisfied by showing that a preference for one sex is a "reasonable occupational qualification" for the job before an exemption to s. 16(1) can be granted, they are clearly wrong.

[38]    In
Saskatchewan Social Services (Corrections Branch)

(1980),
1980 CanLII 3933 (SK HRT)
,
1 C.H.R.R. D/49
, the Commission granted several exemptions to s. 16(1) with respect to the gender of prison guards. In regard to the then existing male penitentiaries, which had open showers and unscreened toilets, a blanket exemption was granted, subject to reconsideration, to prevent women from occupying positions as prison guards. In the newly constructed penitentiaries, where more consideration was given to inmate privacy, an exemption was granted in favour of male prison guards only in areas where nudity or searching of the person was unavoidable. A similar exemption was granted in favour of female prison guards in all-female institutions. Once again, the justification for the exemption was privacy and public decency and no reference was made to s. 16(7).

3.    Did the Commission commit an error of law apparent on the face of the record in determining that
s. 48
of the
Code
was applicable for adjudicating such an exemption request?

[39]    On November 25, 1994, SEIU wrote a letter to the Director of the Commission requesting a reconsideration pursuant to s. 47(2) of the exemption order granted to the Melfort and District Pioneer Home. It is clear from the decision of the Commission that the reconsideration of the exemption order proceeded on the basis of s. 48.

[40]    SEIU was clearly incorrect in asking for a reconsideration under s. 47(2) of an exemption granted under s. 48. If a party interested in an exemption order alleges that the rationale for the exemption no longer exists, the proper section for a reconsideration is s. 48(2) (
Saskatchewan Social Services Corrections Branch
v.
Saskatchewan Government Employees' Union

(1982),
1982 CanLII 4901 (SK HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/1047
at D/1049.

[41]    Furthermore, s. 47 deals exclusively with affirmative action programs designed to alleviate disadvantages in employment situations among various groups in society on a long-term basis.

4.    Did the Commission make an error of law in determining that the Board discharged the burden of proof required to justify the exemption pursuant to
s. 48
of the
Code
?

[42]    The burden of proof in an application for an exemption under s. 48 is discharged where the employer establishes to the Commission's satisfaction that it is "necessary or advisable" that the exemption be granted.

[43]    Where the employer relies on the objective of promoting the inherent dignity and autonomy of the individual, the justification will be met if the exemption sought promotes public decency and privacy.

5.    Did the Commission make an error of law in failing to determine that such exemption was "necessary and advisable" as required by the provisions of
s. 48
of the
Code
?

[44]    It is clear that the Commission did consider whether the exemption was "necessary and advisable" throughout their analysis. The Commission's recognition of the balance that must be struck between the fundamental objects of the
Code
,
their specific consideration of the basic principles of dignity and autonomy, their determination of whether the circumstances that give rise to the original exemption continued to exist and their finding that "some male residents want male attendants to provide their personal care" all involve valid considerations of whether the exemption was "necessary and advisable".

6.    Did the Commission make a jurisdictional error in determining that the provisions of the
Code
protect private rights and therefore ought to be extended to residents who live within institutions through recognition of their preferences?

[45]    The
Code
does recognize and protect a person's private rights in the sense that the
Code
's anti-discrimination provision does not apply within an individual's home.

[46]    The unique situation facing residents at Nirvana is that special care homes fall on the border of the public and private sphere. The Commission described the situation facing the residents at Nirvana in its decision at p. 11 [D/64, para. 22]:

From the perspective of employees who work in them, they are public institutions supported by taxpayers' money and subject to labour laws, collective agreements and other regulatory provisions. From the perspective of the residents, however, these institutions are their homes, and the privacy they have within these places is the only privacy they have. Unlike other Saskatchewan people, residents of institutions exercise very few choices within their private [spheres].

[47]    In my view the Commission therefore must balance the rights of employees to be protected by the anti-discrimination provisions in the
Code
against the rights of residents to be free from these same provisions in their private lives. The balance in the circumstances of special care homes clearly favours the residents and thus justifies protecting their private rights which have also fallen into the public sphere. The Commission recognized the importance of the private rights of the residents of Nirvana in its decision at p. 12 [D/64–D/65, paras. 25–26]:

Another factor i[n] the residents' situation is critical to the reasons for this category of exemptions. The choice the residents wish to make is not a trivial or pernicious one, but one relating to bodily integrity. Personal care and other activities covered by this category of exemptions (such as strip searches) necessarily involve touching of an individual. Touching someone without her or his consent is an assault, and is both a civil and criminal wrong. Many residents have no choice but to tolerate touching by others if they require assistance with personal care, and to tolerate it every day on a long-term basis.

Moreover, the touching is not casual contact ... but touching of the most intimate and often invasive kind, involving nudity and exposure of private areas of the body.

[48]    In my view it would be inimical to the objects of the
Code
to deny residents the protection of their personal dignity and privacy while affording such protection to prisoners in Saskatchewan penitentiaries.

CONCLUSION

[49]    The legal principles contained in the
Code
make it clear that anti-discrimination rights are not absolute in the context of employment. Both ss. 16(7) and 48 contain qualifications and exemptions. One of the objects of the
Code
is respect for the inherent dignity and autonomy of the individual. Following this object the Commission has, in the past, granted a number of exemptions involving the personal care of individuals confined to institutions such as nursing homes. The Commission, in my view, is exercising its discretion judicially when it permits the homes to hire a man or a woman (as required by circumstances) in order to offer residents a choice about the sex of employees providing personal care. I agree with the Commission that personal care involves bodily functions of an intimate nature and as residents in facilities have already lost a great deal of independence in their personal lives, respect for their dignity compels offering them a choice, if possible, about the sex of their personal caregiver. Therefore, in my view, not only is the decision of the Commission not patently unreasonable, it is correct.

[50]    I would be amiss if I did not acknowledge the written briefs filed by both counsel which were of great assistance to the Court.

[51]    The application by SEIU is therefore dismissed with costs.
